Adaptive Budget Allocation in LLM-Augmented Surveys

Zikun Ye    Jiameng Lyu ††thanks: Corresponding Author: Jiameng Lyu    Rui Tao
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) can generate survey responses at low cost, but their reliability varies substantially across questions and is unknown before data collection. Deploying LLMs in surveys still requires costly human responses for verification and correction. How should a limited human-labeling budget be allocated across questions in real time? We propose an adaptive allocation algorithm that learns which questions are hardest for the LLM while simultaneously collecting human responses. Each human label serves a dual role: it improves the estimate for that question and reveals how well the LLM predicts human responses on it. The algorithm directs more budget to questions where the LLM is least reliable, without requiring any prior knowledge of question-level LLM accuracy. We prove that the allocation gap relative to the best possible allocation vanishes as the budget grows, and validate the approach on both synthetic data and a real survey dataset with 68 questions and over 2,000 respondents. On real survey data, the standard practice of allocating human labels uniformly across questions wastes 10–12% of the budget relative to the optimal; our algorithm reduces this waste to 2–6%, and the advantage grows as questions become more heterogeneous in LLM prediction quality. The algorithm achieves the same estimation quality as traditional uniform sampling with fewer human samples, requires no pilot study, and is backed by formal performance guarantees validated on real survey data. More broadly, the framework applies whenever scarce human oversight must be allocated across tasks where LLM reliability is unknown.

1 Introduction

Generative AI is increasingly used as a low-cost first-pass layer in data collection workflows: it can produce predictions, content, and synthetic responses at scale, but its reliability varies sharply across tasks and is rarely known before deployment (Peng et al. 2025, Ziems et al. 2024, Dominguez-Olmedo et al. 2024). As a result, organizations still need human verification and correction, yet human effort is costly, slow, and limited. A central operational question is how to allocate scarce human oversight across tasks in real time so that AI creates value without compromising quality.

LLM-augmented surveys provide a concrete and important instance of this problem. Survey platforms and market research firms are exploring LLM-generated respondent panels to reduce fielding costs and accelerate data collection (Brand et al. 2023, Argyle et al. 2023, Wang et al. 2024). However, LLMs cannot reliably replace human respondents: their predictions exhibit systematic biases and question-type-dependent accuracy (Motoki et al. 2024, Brucks and Toubia 2025, Toubia et al. 2025). A more effective approach is to combine LLM predictions with human responses, using cheap LLM output to reduce the number of human labels needed while correcting for LLM errors. Several frameworks formalize this idea, including prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al. 2023a, Angelopoulos et al. 2023b, PPI;), fine-tuning-then-rectification (Wang et al. 2025), and mixed human-LLM designs (Broska et al. 2025, Yin and Xin 2025).

These hybrid frameworks reduce but do not eliminate the need for human labels: human responses remain the ground truth that corrects LLM bias, and collecting them is costly and slow. In practice, a study often involves many estimation targets sharing a limited labeling budget, such as questions in a survey, product concepts in a market test, or strata in a stratified study. A key challenge is that LLM prediction quality varies dramatically across survey questions (Dominguez-Olmedo et al. 2024, Peng et al. 2025, Toubia et al. 2025), and this heterogeneity persists even after prompt engineering or fine-tuning (Wang et al. 2025, Krsteski et al. 2025). This variation directly determines how many human labels each question requires: questions where LLM predictions closely match human responses need few human labels, while questions where they diverge need many more (Neyman 1934). When this variation is large, directing more of the budget to the harder targets can substantially reduce the aggregate estimation error compared to allocating labels uniformly. When the variation is small, uniform allocation is near-optimal, and no adaptive method is needed.

In practice, however, how well the LLM performs on each question is unknown before data collection begins. Estimating this for every question would require a costly pilot study, and such estimates may not transfer across populations, prompts, or survey instruments. At the same time, in online data collection, human responses arrive sequentially, which makes it feasible to adapt the allocation in real time: the survey designer can use early responses to learn which questions are hard for the LLM and redirect subsequent budget accordingly. This motivates the central research question of this paper: how should a survey designer adaptively allocate a finite human-labeling budget across questions when question-level LLM accuracy is unknown before data collection begins?

We address this question by developing an online learning framework for budget allocation within PPI. The key quantity governing the allocation is the variance of the human-LLM residual for each question, denoted AqA_{q}: it captures how much of the response variation the LLM fails to predict. We design a UCB-based algorithm that learns {Aq}\{A_{q}\} online while allocating the budget, and prove it achieves O⁡(ln⁡B/B2)O(\ln B/B^{2}) regret relative to the Neyman oracle. We compare UCB against several natural benchmarks on both synthetic and real survey data, where it consistently closes the majority of the gap between uniform allocation and the infeasible oracle.

More precisely, AqA_{q} is the variance of the residual between human and LLM responses: when LLM predictions closely match human responses, AqA_{q} is small and few human labels suffice; when they diverge, AqA_{q} is large and more labels are needed. If {Aq}\{A_{q}\} were known, the optimal allocation would follow the classical Neyman square-root rule (Neyman 1934), directing human labels in proportion to wq​Aq/cq\sqrt{w_{q}A_{q}/c_{q}}, where wqw_{q} is the importance weight and cqc_{q} is the per-label cost. The challenge is that they are unknown before data collection and must be learned from the same data used for estimation.

To address this, we propose an Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) allocation policy that learns rectification difficulties online while allocating the budget. At each step, the algorithm selects the question with the highest uncertainty-adjusted marginal efficiency: a UCB index that balances the current difficulty estimate against a confidence bound reflecting estimation uncertainty. Each human label serves a dual role: it improves the population mean estimate for that question and simultaneously reveals information about the question’s difficulty through the paired human-LLM residual. The algorithm requires no prior knowledge of LLM accuracy, is computationally lightweight, and can serve as a practical alternative to uniform sampling. We prove that this policy achieves O⁡(ln⁡B/B2)O(\ln B/B^{2}) regret relative to the Neyman oracle for both PPI and PPI++ estimators, meaning that the efficiency loss from not knowing the difficulties vanishes rapidly as the budget grows.

We compare UCB against several allocation strategies on both synthetic and real survey data. In controlled synthetic experiments (Q=100Q{=}100), UCB tracks the oracle closely at every budget level, and its regret follows the predicted O⁡(ln⁡B/B2)O(\ln B/B^{2}) rate. The synthetic results also reveal that the value of adaptive allocation is driven by heterogeneity in {Aq}\{A_{q}\} rather than by overall LLM quality: improving LLM accuracy reduces the MSE for all strategies equally, but it does not change which one performs best.

We then evaluate on real survey data from the Twin-2K-500 digital twin dataset (Toubia et al. 2025), which contains over 2,000 US respondents across 500+ survey questions; we use the 68-question retest battery from Wave 4, spanning cognitive heuristic tasks, behavioral economics experiments, and political opinion items, each with paired human and LLM responses. We compare UCB against four benchmarks: the oracle (Neyman allocation with known difficulties), uniform allocation (equal samples per question), ε\varepsilon-greedy (a standard adaptive baseline from the bandit literature), and explore-then-commit (ETC), which mimics the common practice of running a pilot study before committing to a fixed allocation. All policies use the same PPI++ estimator and differ only in how they allocate human labels. UCB achieves the lowest MSE among all implementable policies at every budget level. The standard uniform allocation (equal samples per question) wastes 10–12% of the budget relative to the oracle; UCB reduces this waste to 2–6%, with the gap shrinking as the budget grows. Beyond the baseline, we systematically vary importance weights and sampling costs and find that UCB maintains a gap of approximately 4% regardless of how heterogeneous the weights or costs are, while uniform allocation degrades substantially. We also vary the degree of heterogeneity in rectification difficulties and confirm the same pattern as in the synthetic experiments: the value of adaptive allocation grows monotonically with heterogeneity, and when all questions have similar difficulty, uniform allocation is near-optimal.

1.1 Related Literature

LLM-augmented surveys and sample allocation. A growing literature studies the use of LLMs as synthetic survey respondents (Argyle et al. 2023, Brand et al. 2023, Ye et al. 2025, Wang et al. 2024, Li et al. 2024, Peng et al. 2025, Toubia et al. 2025, Ziems et al. 2024, Motoki et al. 2024, Brucks and Toubia 2025). Several frameworks have been proposed to combine human labels with LLM predictions, including prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al. 2023a, Angelopoulos et al. 2023b, Mozer 2026, Ji et al. 2025, Vafa et al. 2025, PPI;), fine-tuning-then-rectification (Wang et al. 2025), and mixed human-LLM designs (Broska et al. 2025, Yin and Xin 2025, Huang et al. 2025). These studies focus on how to combine human and LLM data for a given question. Our work addresses the complementary across-question allocation decision. Classical Neyman allocation (Neyman 1934) assigns samples to strata in proportion to their variance-to-cost ratio, and a rich literature on adaptive survey design shares the philosophy of directing scarce respondent effort where it is most informative (Toubia et al. 2003, Raghunathan and Grizzle 1995, e.g.,). In LLM-augmented surveys, Neyman allocation requires the variance of the human-LLM residual for each question, which is unknown before data collection. Our work learns these residual variances online with formal regret guarantees.

Online learning and bandit algorithms. Our problem of sequentially allocating a budget across estimation targets under uncertainty connects to the multi-armed bandit literature (Auer et al. 2002, Lattimore and Szepesvári 2020), its resource-constrained variants (Badanidiyuru et al. 2018, Agrawal and Devanur 2016, bandits with knapsacks;), and UCB-based approaches in operational settings such as dynamic pricing (Cohen et al. 2025). However, these formulations target cumulative reward maximization, whereas our objective is to minimize the terminal aggregate estimation error across a portfolio of estimands. We adopt a terminal-MSE-gap regret definition similar to that of Carpentier et al. (2015), who model stratified sampling as a bandit problem. However, we focus on the LLM-augmented survey problem, where the information source is the PPI/PPI++ residual from paired human-LLM observations. Furthermore, we must handle heterogeneous costs in both PPI/PPI++ settings, and address the additional challenge of jointly learning the tuning parameter and the residual variance for each question in the PPI++ setting. In a related vein, Li et al. (2026) study sequential hypothesis testing with heterogeneous LLMs, and Simchi-Levi and Wang (2025) study the trade-off between regret minimization and statistical inference in bandit problems.

Human-AI collaboration. More broadly, our problem connects to the growing literature on how to allocate human oversight across AI-generated outputs. Dai and Swaminathan (2025) identify human-AI interaction as a central pillar of AI in operations, emphasizing the need for frameworks that determine when and where human intervention adds value. Fügener et al. (2026) study when AI should automate tasks versus augment human judgment, showing that the optimal division depends on the type of complementarity between human and AI capabilities. DiSorbo et al. (2025) study how to direct human attention to AI predictions most likely to be unreliable, using warnings and endorsements to improve human-AI collaboration. Related work includes fairness in human-AI collaboration (Ge et al. 2023) and trust in human-robot decision-making (Bhat et al. 2025). Our work contributes to this literature by providing an online algorithm that learns where human oversight is most needed and allocates effort accordingly, with formal performance guarantees.

Organization of the paper. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 formalizes the problem. Section 3 presents the UCB algorithm and its regret guarantee. Section 4 extends the framework to the PPI++ estimator. Sections 5 and 6 validate the approach on synthetic and real survey data, respectively. Section 7 concludes. Online Appendix A extends the allocation framework to general MM-estimation targets.

2 Problem Formulation

In the following, we formalize our LLM-augmented survey design problem. We first introduce the survey design setting in Section 2.1. We then review prediction-powered inference (PPI), highlighting the variance of the LLM prediction residual, called rectification difficulty, that governs estimation variance in Section 2.2. Last, we frame our problem as an online learning problem, in which rectification difficulties are unknown and must be learned sequentially, and define regret relative to the oracle in Section 2.3.

2.1 Survey Design Setting

Consider a set of target survey questions 𝒯={1,…,Q}\mathcal{T}=\{1,\ldots,Q\}. For each question q∈𝒯q\in\mathcal{T} and respondent ii, let Xq,i∈𝒳X_{q,i}\in\mathcal{X} denote the features associated with question qq and respondent ii (e.g., question text, response options, and respondent demographics), and let Yq,i∈𝒴Y_{q,i}\in\mathcal{Y} denote the human response (e.g., a rating or choice indicator). Within each question, observations are i.i.d. from a question-specific population distribution:

(Xq,i,Yq,i)​∼i.i.d.​𝒫q.(X_{q,i},Y_{q,i})\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathcal{P}_{q}.

We write 𝒫qX\mathcal{P}^{X}_{q} for the marginal covariate distribution of XqX_{q} and 𝒫q(⋅∣X)\mathcal{P}_{q}(\cdot\mid X) for the conditional response distribution, so that 𝒫q=𝒫qX⊗𝒫q(⋅∣X)\mathcal{P}_{q}=\mathcal{P}^{X}_{q}\otimes\mathcal{P}_{q}(\cdot\mid X).

The estimand is the population mean response θq∗:=E𝒫q​[Yq]\theta_{q}^{*}:=\mathrm{E}_{\mathcal{P}_{q}}[Y_{q}]. Given importance weights {wq}q=1Q\{w_{q}\}_{q=1}^{Q} of survey questions, the survey design goal is to choose sample sizes {nq}q=1Q\{n_{q}\}_{q=1}^{Q} of survey questions to minimize the weighted aggregate MSE:

min⁡∑q=1Q{nq}⁡wq​E​[(θ^q−θq∗)2]s.t.∑q=1Qcq​nq≤B.\min_{\{n_{q}\}}\sum_{q=1}^{Q}w_{q}\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[(\hat{\theta}_{q}-\theta_{q}^{*})^{2}\right]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{q=1}^{Q}c_{q}\,n_{q}\leq B.

The per-label cost for question qq is cq>0c_{q}>0, and the total human-label budget is BB. Throughout, we use individual survey questions as the allocation unit and scalar population means as the estimand. The framework extends in two directions. First, the allocation unit can be a question module rather than a single question: many surveys group questions into thematic modules and assign each respondent to one or more modules, as in split questionnaire designs (Raghunathan and Grizzle 1995). Section 6.5 validates module-level allocation on real data. Second, the estimand can be vector-valued (e.g., regression coefficients or conjoint partworths), with the scalar difficulty derived from a sandwich covariance; Online Appendix A develops this MM-estimation extension with a synthetic data experiment of the MNL choice model estimation for illustration.

2.2 Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI) and Rectification Difficulty

An LLM provides a low-cost predictor f:𝒳→𝒴f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}, yielding a surrogate prediction Yq,iLLM:=f⁡(Xq,i)Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q,i}:=f(X_{q,i}). For each question qq, the researcher has access to two data sources: a labeled sample of nqn_{q} costly human responses, each paired with an LLM prediction on the same features, and an unlabeled synthetic pool of mqm_{q} LLM predictions, obtained by querying the LLM at low cost and large scale without collecting any human responses. Prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al. 2023a, PPI;) combines these two sources into an unbiased estimator for θq∗\theta_{q}^{*}:

θ^qPPI=1mq​∑j=1mqYq,jLLM⏟LLM prediction (unlabeled)+1nq​∑i=1nq(Yq,i−Yq,iLLM)⏟rectification (labeled),\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{PPI}}_{q}=\underbrace{\frac{1}{m_{q}}\sum_{j=1}^{m_{q}}Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q,j}}_{\text{LLM prediction (unlabeled)}}\;+\;\underbrace{\frac{1}{n_{q}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{q}}\left(Y_{q,i}-Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q,i}\right)}_{\text{rectification (labeled)}},

where jj indexes the unlabeled synthetic pool and ii indexes the labeled sample. The first term averages the LLM’s predictions across the synthetic pool. The second term corrects for the LLM’s systematic bias using paired human–LLM observations: each difference Y~q,i:=Yq,i−Yq,iLLM\tilde{Y}_{q,i}:=Y_{q,i}-Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q,i} isolates the LLM’s prediction error on respondent ii, and averaging these residuals yields an unbiased correction since E⁡[Y~q]=θq∗−E⁡[f⁡(Xq)]\mathrm{E}[\tilde{Y}_{q}]=\theta_{q}^{*}-\mathrm{E}[f(X_{q})] exactly offsets the LLM bias in the first term.

Since the labeled and synthetic samples are independent, the variance decomposes as

Var⁡(θ^qPPI)=1mq​Var​(YqLLM)+1nq​Var​(Yq−YqLLM).\mathrm{Var}\!\big(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{PPI}}_{q}\big)=\frac{1}{m_{q}}\mathrm{Var}\!\big(Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}\big)\;+\;\frac{1}{n_{q}}\mathrm{Var}\!\big(Y_{q}-Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}\big). (1)

Define the rectification difficulty of question qq as the residual variance

Aq:=Var⁡(Y~q)=Var⁡(Yq−YqLLM).A_{q}:=\mathrm{Var}(\tilde{Y}_{q})=\mathrm{Var}\!\big(Y_{q}-Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}\big).

Since synthetic responses can be generated cheaply at any scale, we work in the synthetic-data-rich (SDR) regime and set mq→∞m_{q}\to\infty for theoretical analysis. This is without loss of generality: the synthetic pool size mqm_{q} is not a decision variable and can be chosen independently of the human-label allocation {nq}\{n_{q}\}. As mq→∞m_{q}\to\infty, the first term in Eq. (1) vanishes and the PPI estimation variance reduces to

Var⁡(θ^qPPI)=Aqnq,\mathrm{Var}\!\big(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{PPI}}_{q}\big)=\frac{A_{q}}{n_{q}},

which implies that optimal survey allocation is governed by {Aq}\{A_{q}\}.

2.3 Online Learning Framework and Regret

We now frame the budget allocation problem as an online learning problem. Since θ^qPPI\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{PPI}}_{q} is unbiased, its MSE equals its variance, so the design objective from Section 2.1 reduces to minimizing ∑qwq​Var​(θ^qPPI)=∑qwq​Aq/nq\sum_{q}w_{q}\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{PPI}}_{q})=\sum_{q}w_{q}A_{q}/n_{q} under the SDR regime. If the rectification difficulties {Aq}\{A_{q}\} were known, this becomes

min⁡∑q=1Q{nq}⁡wq​Aqnqs.t.∑q=1Qcq​nq≤B.\min_{\{n_{q}\}}\sum_{q=1}^{Q}w_{q}\frac{A_{q}}{n_{q}}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{q=1}^{Q}c_{q}n_{q}\leq B.

The optimal solution follows a Neyman-type square-root allocation rule:

nq∗=B∑j=1Qwj​Aj​cj​wq​Aqcq,q∈𝒯.n_{q}^{*}=\frac{B}{\sum_{j=1}^{Q}\sqrt{w_{j}A_{j}c_{j}}}\sqrt{\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{c_{q}}},\qquad q\in\mathcal{T}. (2)

Thus, questions that are more important (large wqw_{q}), harder to rectify (large AqA_{q}), or cheaper (small cqc_{q}) receive more human labels. We refer to Eq. (2) as the oracle allocation.

However, this oracle is not directly implementable because it requires knowledge of {Aq}\{A_{q}\}. Since Aq=Var⁡(Yq−YqLLM)A_{q}=\mathrm{Var}(Y_{q}-Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}) depends on the joint distribution of human responses and LLM predictions, it is unknown before any human data are collected and varies across questions, populations, and LLM models. One could run a pilot survey to estimate {Aq}\{A_{q}\} before committing to an allocation, but this requires choosing how much of the budget to spend on the pilot versus the main study, and pilot estimates from a small sample may be unreliable. This motivates an online formulation that learns {Aq}\{A_{q}\} while allocating the budget, avoiding the need for a separate pilot phase.

We model data collection as a sequential allocation process. At each step tt, a policy selects a question qt∈𝒯q_{t}\in\mathcal{T} based on past observations, collects one additional human response for that question (paying cost cqtc_{q_{t}}), queries the LLM on the same covariates, and obtains one residual sample Y~qt,t=Yqt,t−Yqt,tLLM\tilde{Y}_{q_{t},t}=Y_{q_{t},t}-Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q_{t},t}. Let nq,tn_{q,t} be the number of human–LLM pairs collected for question qq up to time tt, and let nq,Bn_{q,B} be the final allocation to question qq when the algorithm terminates.

An adaptive policy π={πt}\pi=\{\pi_{t}\} maps the history ht−1={(qs,Yqs,s,Yqs,sLLM)}s=1t−1h_{t-1}=\{(q_{s},Y_{q_{s},s},Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q_{s},s})\}_{s=1}^{t-1} to the next question qtq_{t}. Because {Aq}\{A_{q}\} are unknown, the policy faces an exploration–exploitation trade-off: sampling a question to reduce uncertainty in its difficulty estimate versus allocating budget to questions that appear most impactful under current estimates.

We measure performance by regret, which is the gap between the expected terminal objective achieved by π\pi and that of the oracle allocation:

ℛ⁡(B):=Eπ​[∑q=1Qwq​Aqnq,B]−∑q=1Qwq​Aqnq∗.\mathcal{R}(B):=\mathrm{E}_{\pi}\!\left[\sum_{q=1}^{Q}w_{q}\frac{A_{q}}{n_{q,B}}\right]-\sum_{q=1}^{Q}w_{q}\frac{A_{q}}{n_{q}^{*}}.

The goal is to design an online allocation policy with sublinear regret as BB grows. The next section develops a UCB-based algorithm that learns {Aq}\{A_{q}\} from PPI residuals and achieves ℛ⁡(B)=O⁡(ln⁡B/B2)\mathcal{R}(B)=O(\ln B/B^{2}).

We note that the LLM augmentation and the adaptive allocation address complementary aspects of the problem. The LLM augmentation via PPI reduces the per-question variance from Var⁡(Yq)\mathrm{Var}(Y_{q}) to AqA_{q}, lowering the overall number of human labels needed. The adaptive allocation exploits heterogeneity in {Aq}\{A_{q}\} across questions to further improve efficiency. Importantly, the allocation problem retains the same structure with or without LLM predictions. Without PPI, the estimator for each question is the sample mean Y¯q\bar{Y}_{q} with per-question variance Var⁡(Yq)/nq\mathrm{Var}(Y_{q})/n_{q}; the allocation-relevant quantity is simply Var⁡(Yq)\mathrm{Var}(Y_{q}), playing the same role as AqA_{q}. With PPI, the variance reduces to Aq/nqA_{q}/n_{q} where Aq=Var⁡(Yq−YqLLM)A_{q}=\mathrm{Var}(Y_{q}-Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}) can be substantially smaller than Var⁡(Yq)\mathrm{Var}(Y_{q}) for questions where the LLM is informative. In both cases, the online allocation problem has the same ⋅/nq\cdot/n_{q} structure; the adaptive algorithm we develop in the next section applies to both settings. The case without LLM predictions corresponds to the classical adaptive stratified sampling problem studied in Carpentier et al. (2015).

3 Algorithm Design and Regret Analysis

We first motivate the algorithm design through a marginal-efficiency interpretation of the oracle allocation in Section 3.1, then construct the UCB index that replaces unknown difficulties with confidence-adjusted estimates in Section 3.2, and present the full algorithm in Section 3.3. Section 3.4 establishes the regret guarantee.

3.1 Oracle Case with Known AqA_{q}: Marginal-Efficiency Interpretation

Recall from Section 2 that Var⁡(θ^qPPI)=Aq/nq\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{PPI}}_{q})=A_{q}/n_{q}. To motivate our adaptive approach, we first analyze the case where the rectification difficulties AqA_{q} are known, but the budget is allocated sequentially. We frame this through the lens of Marginal Efficiency.

To build intuition, consider two survey questions with A1=4A_{1}=4, A2=1A_{2}=1 and equal weights and costs (wq=cq=1w_{q}=c_{q}=1). The oracle allocates n1∗=2​n2∗n_{1}^{*}=2n_{2}^{*} (proportional to Aq\sqrt{A_{q}}). Suppose both questions currently have nq=10n_{q}=10 samples. The marginal efficiency of adding one more sample to question 1 is A1/n12=4/100=0.04A_{1}/n_{1}^{2}=4/100=0.04, versus A2/n22=1/100=0.01A_{2}/n_{2}^{2}=1/100=0.01 for question 2. The greedy rule correctly directs the next sample to the harder question.

More generally, consider the current state at round tt, where each question qq has been allocated nq,tn_{q,t} samples. If we were to allocate one additional sample to question qq, the objective function ∑qwq​Aqnq\sum_{q}w_{q}\frac{A_{q}}{n_{q}} would decrease. The Marginal Variance Reduction is given by the negative partial derivative with respect to nqn_{q}:

−∂∂nq​(wq​Aqnq)=wq​Aqnq2-\frac{\partial}{\partial n_{q}}\left(w_{q}\frac{A_{q}}{n_{q}}\right)=\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{n_{q}^{2}}

Since each sample for question qq costs cqc_{q}, we define the Marginal Efficiency Index ℐq,t\mathcal{I}_{q,t} as the variance reduction per unit of currency spent:

ℐq,t∗=Marginal Variance ReductionMarginal Cost=wq​Aqcq​nq,t2.\mathcal{I}_{q,t}^{*}=\frac{\text{Marginal Variance Reduction}}{\text{Marginal Cost}}=\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{c_{q}n_{q,t}^{2}}.

A policy that greedily selects q=arg⁡max⁡ℐq,t∗q=\arg\max\mathcal{I}_{q,t}^{*} at each step converges to the optimal oracle allocation nq∗n_{q}^{*}, because the greedy rule drives the system toward a state where the marginal efficiency wq​Aq/(cq​nq2)w_{q}A_{q}/(c_{q}n_{q}^{2}) is equalized across all qq, which is precisely the first-order condition of the Lagrangian of the static optimization problem.

3.2 UCB Index Construction

In practice, AqA_{q} is unknown. The key role of the LLM is to produce cheap paired predictions f⁡(X)f(X) so that each costly human label immediately yields a variance-relevant residual sample Y~=Y−f⁡(X)\tilde{Y}=Y-f(X). For each question qq, let nq,tn_{q,t} be the number of human labels collected up to round tt, and let A^q,t\widehat{A}_{q,t} be the unbiased sample variance of {Y~q,i}i=1nq,t\{\tilde{Y}_{q,i}\}_{i=1}^{n_{q,t}}:

A^q,t=1nq,t−1​∑i=1nq,t(Y~q,i−Y~¯q,t)2.\widehat{A}_{q,t}=\frac{1}{n_{q,t}-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{q,t}}(\tilde{Y}_{q,i}-\bar{\tilde{Y}}_{q,t})^{2}. (3)

A naive plug-in greedy approach using the empirical variance A^q,t\widehat{A}_{q,t} can under-sample a question whose true AqA_{q} is high but whose initial A^q,t\widehat{A}_{q,t} was accidentally low.

To address this, we use the Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) principle. For a bounded random variable Y~\tilde{Y} with range RR, the deviation of the sample variance from the true variance is controlled by:

Aq≤Aq,tUCB,A_{q}\leq A^{\mathrm{UCB}}_{q,t},

where

Aq,tUCB:=A^q,t+2​R​2​A^q,t​ln⁡(2/δq,t)nq,t−1+2​R2​ln⁡(2/δq,t)nq,t−1.\displaystyle A^{\mathrm{UCB}}_{q,t}:=\widehat{A}_{q,t}+2R\sqrt{\frac{2\widehat{A}_{q,t}\ln(2/\delta_{q,t})}{n_{q,t}-1}}+\frac{2R^{2}\ln(2/\delta_{q,t})}{n_{q,t}-1}.

We define the UCB index to prioritize questions that either have high estimated difficulty (exploitation) or high estimation uncertainty (exploration):

ℐq,tUCB=wq​Aq,tUCBcq​nq,t2.\mathcal{I}_{q,t}^{\mathrm{UCB}}=\frac{w_{q}A^{\mathrm{UCB}}_{q,t}}{c_{q}n_{q,t}^{2}}.

The empirical Bernstein bound above contains the question-dependent A^q,t\widehat{A}_{q,t}: when the LLM is accurate (small A^q,t\widehat{A}_{q,t}), the confidence width shrinks faster, so “easy” questions exit the exploration phase sooner and stop consuming budget. This variance-adaptive tightening allows the algorithm to concentrate its exploration budget on questions with genuinely high uncertainty, echoing the structure of the Neyman rule that allocates proportionally to Aq\sqrt{A_{q}}.

3.3 Algorithm Description

The algorithm enforces an initialization of K≥2K\geq 2 labels per question to make A^q,t\widehat{A}_{q,t} well-defined, then repeatedly allocates the next human query to the question with the largest UCB index. Each allocation uses the LLM on the same covariate/prompt to produce a paired prediction and thus an immediate residual update. It then proceeds sequentially until the remaining budget falls below maxq⁡cq\max_{q}c_{q}.

The adaptive phase stops once the remaining budget falls below cmaxc_{\max}, so every question compared in the UCB arg⁡max\arg\max is feasible throughout the phase. The unspent remainder RemB∈[0,cmax)\mathrm{Rem}_{B}\in[0,c_{\max}) is bounded and asymptotically negligible relative to BB.

3.4 Regret Analysis

We now state the main theoretical guarantee for Algorithm 1. Recall Aq:=Var⁡(Y~q)A_{q}:=\mathrm{Var}(\tilde{Y}_{q}) with Y~q:=Yq−f⁡(Xq)\tilde{Y}_{q}:=Y_{q}-f(X_{q}). Let nq,Bn_{q,B} be the total number of human labels allocated to question qq when the algorithm stops under budget BB. Define cmin:=minq⁡cqc_{\min}:=\min_{q}c_{q}, cmax:=maxq⁡cqc_{\max}:=\max_{q}c_{q}, and Tmax:=⌊B/cmin⌋T_{\max}:=\lfloor B/c_{\min}\rfloor. The oracle allocation is

nq∗=B∑j=1Qwj​Aj​cj​wq​Aqcq,Λ:=∑j=1Qwj​Aj​cj,βq:=nq∗B=wq​Aq/cqΛ.n_{q}^{*}=\frac{B}{\sum_{j=1}^{Q}\sqrt{w_{j}A_{j}c_{j}}}\sqrt{\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{c_{q}}},\qquad\Lambda:=\sum_{j=1}^{Q}\sqrt{w_{j}A_{j}c_{j}},\qquad\beta_{q}:=\frac{n_{q}^{*}}{B}=\frac{\sqrt{w_{q}A_{q}/c_{q}}}{\Lambda}.

The regret is defined as

ℛ⁡(B):=E⁡[∑q=1Qwq​Aqnq,B]−∑q=1Qwq​Aqnq∗.\mathcal{R}(B):=\mathrm{E}\!\left[\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{n_{q,B}}\right]-\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{n_{q}^{*}}. (4)

We impose two assumptions for the theoretical analysis of Algorithm 1. Throughout, we assume wq>0w_{q}>0 and cq>0c_{q}>0 for all qq, and that the budget is large enough for initialization: B≥∑q=1Qcq​KB\geq\sum_{q=1}^{Q}c_{q}K.

{assumption}

For every q∈[Q]q\in[Q] and every draw ii, the residual satisfies Y~q=Yq−YqLLM∈[L,U]\tilde{Y}_{q}=Y_{q}-Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}\in[L,U] almost surely with range R:=U−L<∞R:=U-L<\infty.

{assumption}

We assume Amin:=minq⁡Aq>0A_{\min}:=\min_{q}A_{q}>0, where Aq:=Var⁡(Yq−YqLLM)A_{q}:=\mathrm{Var}(Y_{q}-Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}). Assumption 3.4 requires the PPI residual Y~q=Yq−YqLLM\tilde{Y}_{q}=Y_{q}-Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q} to be bounded, which is needed to apply finite-sample variance concentration inequalities. This holds whenever survey responses are bounded, as in Likert scales, binary choices, or bounded-range ratings. Assumption 3.4 requires that no question is perfectly predicted by the LLM, so that every question retains some residual variance. If the LLM predicted a question perfectly, that question would require no human labels and could be excluded from the allocation problem.

With these assumptions, we have the following theoretical guarantee for the regret of Algorithm 1.

Theorem 3.1

Suppose Assumptions 3.4–3.4 hold. Run Algorithm 1 with K≥2K\geq 2. Let Vmax:=∑q=1Qwq​Aq/KV_{\max}:=\sum_{q=1}^{Q}w_{q}A_{q}/K. Then for all sufficiently large BB,

ℛ⁡(B)≤O⁡(ln⁡(Q​Tmax/δ)B2)+δ​Vmax.\mathcal{R}(B)\leq O\left(\frac{\ln(QT_{\max}/\delta)}{B^{2}}\right)+\delta V_{\max}.

In particular, choosing δ=B−2\delta=B^{-2} yields ℛ⁡(B)=O⁡(ln⁡BB2)\mathcal{R}(B)=O\!\left(\frac{\ln B}{B^{2}}\right).

The proof proceeds in three steps. We present the key constructions and results here; complete algebraic details are in Online Appendix B.

Step I: Good Event and Optimism

To control regret, we define a high-probability good event under which the empirical variance concentrates uniformly around the true difficulty for all questions and all rounds. For each (q,s)(q,s), let A~q,s\widetilde{A}_{q,s} denote the sample variance computed from the first ss i.i.d. residuals of question qq. Set δq,s:=δ/(Q​Tmax)\delta_{q,s}:=\delta/(QT_{\max}) and define

ℰ:=⋂q=1Q⋂s=KTmax{|Aq−A~q,s|≤R2​ln⁡(2/δq,s)s−1}.\mathcal{E}:=\bigcap_{q=1}^{Q}\bigcap_{s=K}^{T_{\max}}\left\{\left|\sqrt{A_{q}}-\sqrt{\widetilde{A}_{q,s}}\right|\leq R\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(2/\delta_{q,s})}{s-1}}\right\}. (5)

Since A^q,t=A~q,nq,t\widehat{A}_{q,t}=\widetilde{A}_{q,n_{q,t}}, the event ℰ\mathcal{E} implies the adaptive-time event

ℰ′:=⋂q=1Q⋂t=1Tmax{|Aq−A^q,t|≤R2​ln⁡(2/δq,t)nq,t−1},\mathcal{E}^{\prime}:=\bigcap_{q=1}^{Q}\bigcap_{t=1}^{T_{\max}}\left\{\left|\sqrt{A_{q}}-\sqrt{\widehat{A}_{q,t}}\right|\leq R\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(2/\delta_{q,t})}{n_{q,t}-1}}\right\},

i.e., ℰ⊆ℰ′\mathcal{E}\subseteq\mathcal{E}^{\prime}. Indexing by the deterministic sample count ss avoids optional-stopping complications: nq,tn_{q,t} is random, so a direct union bound over (q,t)(q,t) in ℰ′\mathcal{E}^{\prime} would be invalid, whereas each (q,s)(q,s) in ℰ\mathcal{E} involves a fixed-size i.i.d. sample.

Lemma 3.2

Under Assumption 3.4, P⁡(ℰ)≥1−δ\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{E})\geq 1-\delta.

Proof 3.3

Proof Sketch. By Assumption 3.4, Zq,i:=(Y~q,i−L)/R∈[0,1]Z_{q,i}:=(\tilde{Y}_{q,i}-L)/R\in[0,1]. For each fixed (q,s)(q,s), the square-root variance concentration inequality of Maurer and Pontil (2009) applied to {Zq,i}i=1s\{Z_{q,i}\}_{i=1}^{s} and rescaled gives P⁡(|Aq−A~q,s|>RHS of (5))≤δq,s\mathrm{P}(|\sqrt{A_{q}}-\sqrt{\widetilde{A}_{q,s}}|>\text{RHS of~\eqref{eq:good_event}})\leq\delta_{q,s}. A union bound over at most Q⋅TmaxQ\cdot T_{\max} pairs yields P⁡(ℰc)≤δ\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{E}^{c})\leq\delta.□\square

Optimism.

On ℰ\mathcal{E}, the condition Aq≤A^q,t+ϵ\sqrt{A_{q}}\leq\sqrt{\widehat{A}_{q,t}}+\epsilon implies Aq≤Aq,tUCBA_{q}\leq A^{\mathrm{UCB}}_{q,t}, so the true marginal-efficiency index is upper-bounded by the optimistic index:

ℐq,t∗=wq​Aqcq​nq,t2≤ℐq,tUCB:=wq​Aq,tUCBcq​nq,t2.\mathcal{I}^{*}_{q,t}=\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{c_{q}n_{q,t}^{2}}\leq\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{UCB}}_{q,t}:=\frac{w_{q}A^{\mathrm{UCB}}_{q,t}}{c_{q}n_{q,t}^{2}}.

This ensures that the algorithm never systematically under-samples a question whose true difficulty is high.

Step II: Allocation Gap Bound

On the good event ℰ\mathcal{E}, the UCB selection rule forces the realized allocation to track the oracle proportions. The key argument uses a pigeonhole construction: there exists a question qaq_{a} whose allocation is at least proportional to its oracle share, and the UCB selection rule ensures that every other question qq satisfies ℐq,t∗≤ℐq,tUCB≤ℐqa,tUCB\mathcal{I}^{*}_{q,t}\leq\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{UCB}}_{q,t}\leq\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{UCB}}_{q_{a},t}. Chaining this inequality (see Online Appendix B for the full derivation) yields

|nq,B−nq∗|=O⁡(B​ln⁡(1/δ)),∀q∈[Q].|n_{q,B}-n_{q}^{*}|=O\!\left(\sqrt{B\ln(1/\delta)}\right),\qquad\forall q\in[Q]. (6)

Step III: From Allocation Gaps to Regret

We convert the allocation gaps into regret via a second-order Taylor expansion of fq​(n)=wq​Aq/nf_{q}(n)=w_{q}A_{q}/n around nq∗n_{q}^{*}. Summing over questions:

∑q=1Q[fq​(nq,B)−fq​(nq∗)]=−∑q=1Qwq​Aq(nq∗)2(nq,B−nq∗)⏟Term 1+∑q=1Qwq​Aqξq3​(nq,B−nq∗)2⏟Term 2.\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\left[f_{q}(n_{q,B})-f_{q}(n_{q}^{*})\right]=\underbrace{-\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{(n_{q}^{*})^{2}}(n_{q,B}-n_{q}^{*})}_{\text{Term 1}}+\underbrace{\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{\xi_{q}^{3}}(n_{q,B}-n_{q}^{*})^{2}}_{\text{Term 2}}.

Term 1 telescopes by the optimality condition wq​Aq/(nq∗)2=λ⁡(B)​cqw_{q}A_{q}/(n_{q}^{*})^{2}=\lambda(B)c_{q}, yielding Term 1=λ⁡(B)⋅RemB\text{Term 1}=\lambda(B)\cdot\mathrm{Rem}_{B} where RemB∈[0,cmax)\mathrm{Rem}_{B}\in[0,c_{\max}) is the leftover budget, contributing O⁡(1/B2)O(1/B^{2}). Term 2 is bounded using Eq. (6): each squared gap is O⁡(B​ln⁡B)O(B\ln B), and the 1/ξq3≈1/(nq∗)3∼1/B31/\xi_{q}^{3}\approx 1/(n_{q}^{*})^{3}\sim 1/B^{3} prefactor yields a total of O⁡(ln⁡B/B2)O(\ln B/B^{2}). Combining with P⁡(ℰc)≤δ=B−2\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{E}^{c})\leq\delta=B^{-2} completes the proof.

4 Extension to PPI++

The standard PPI estimator in Section 2.2 subtracts the full LLM prediction from each human response. This improves over the sample mean only when the LLM is sufficiently correlated with human responses: specifically, PPI reduces variance when Cov⁡(Yq,YqLLM)>Var⁡(YqLLM)/2\mathrm{Cov}(Y_{q},Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q})>\mathrm{Var}(Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q})/2. When the LLM is a weak predictor, the rectification difficulty Aq=Var⁡(Yq−YqLLM)A_{q}=\mathrm{Var}(Y_{q}-Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}) can exceed Var⁡(Yq)\mathrm{Var}(Y_{q}), making PPI worse than the sample mean estimator.

PPI++ (Angelopoulos et al. 2023b) addresses this by introducing a tuning parameter λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] that controls how much of the LLM prediction to use. The rectification residual becomes Y−λ​YLLMY-\lambda Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}, where λ\lambda is learned from paired data to minimize residual variance. When λ∗=0\lambda^{*}=0, the estimator ignores the LLM and reduces to the sample mean; when λ∗>0\lambda^{*}>0, it leverages the LLM signal for variance reduction. We now extend our online allocation framework to this setting. Algorithmically, this alters only how we (i) construct residuals and (ii) build a valid UCB for the corresponding difficulty parameter.

4.1 PPI++ Estimator and Tuned Rectification Difficulty

For completeness, we briefly review the PPI++ estimator and the optimal tuning parameter λ∗\lambda^{*}; the material in this subsection is standard and follows Angelopoulos et al. (2023b).

Fix a question q∈[Q]q\in[Q]. Recall that YqLLM=f⁡(Xq)Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}=f(X_{q}), i.e., the LLM-generated counterpart of YqY_{q} introduced earlier. We observe paired samples {(Yq,i,Yq,iLLM)}i≥1\{(Y_{q,i},Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q,i})\}_{i\geq 1} that are i.i.d. across respondents: each pair is an independent draw from the joint distribution of (Yq,YqLLM)(Y_{q},Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}). For any tuning parameter λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1], define the tuned residual

Y~q​(λ):=Yq−λ​YqLLM.\tilde{Y}_{q}(\lambda):=Y_{q}-\lambda Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}.

In the synthetic-data-rich regime (so that the LLM-only mean can be treated as known up to negligible error), the PPI++ estimator of θq∗=E⁡[Yq]\theta_{q}^{*}=\mathrm{E}[Y_{q}] can be written as

θ^qPPI++​(λ)=Y¯q,nq+λ⁡(Y¯q,mqLLM−Y¯q,nqLLM),λ∈[0,1],\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{PPI++}}_{q}(\lambda)=\bar{Y}_{q,n_{q}}+\lambda\left(\bar{Y}^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q,m_{q}}-\bar{Y}^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q,n_{q}}\right),\qquad\lambda\in[0,1],

which is unbiased for any fixed λ\lambda, and when mq→∞m_{q}\to\infty, satisfies

Var⁡(θ^qPPI++​(λ))=Var⁡(Yq−λ​YqLLM)nq.\mathrm{Var}\!\big(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{PPI++}}_{q}(\lambda)\big)=\frac{\mathrm{Var}\!\big(Y_{q}-\lambda Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}\big)}{n_{q}}.

The PPI++ tuning parameter is the clipped population regression coefficient

λq∗:=Π[0,1]​(Cov⁡(Yq,YqLLM)Var⁡(YqLLM)),\lambda_{q}^{*}:=\Pi_{[0,1]}\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(Y_{q},Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q})}{\mathrm{Var}(Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q})}\right), (7)

and the resulting tuned rectification difficulty is

Aq​(λq∗):=Var⁡(Y~q​(λq∗))=Var⁡(Yq−λq∗​YqLLM).A_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*}):=\mathrm{Var}\!\big(\tilde{Y}_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*})\big)=\mathrm{Var}\!\big(Y_{q}-\lambda_{q}^{*}Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}\big).

By optimality of λq∗\lambda_{q}^{*}, Aq​(λq∗)≤Var⁡(Yq−YqLLM)A_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*})\leq\mathrm{Var}(Y_{q}-Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}), i.e., PPI++ is never worse (in asymptotic variance) than standard PPI.

4.2 Algorithm Design with PPI++

Algorithm 2 presents the PPI++ variant of the UCB allocation procedure. Its high-level structure mirrors Algorithm 1: after initializing each question with K≥2K\geq 2 paired samples, the algorithm sequentially allocates human labels to the question with the largest UCB index of marginal-efficiency until the remaining budget falls below maxq⁡cq\max_{q}c_{q}. The key differences from Algorithm 1 are threefold.

  1. 1.

    Residual construction and updating. In standard PPI, each human label yields a fixed residual Y~q,i=Yq,i−Yq,iLLM\tilde{Y}_{q,i}=Y_{q,i}-Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q,i}, and the unknown difficulty Aq=Var⁡(Yq−YqLLM)A_{q}=\mathrm{Var}(Y_{q}-Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}) is estimated by the sample variance of these residuals. In PPI++, the residual is parametrized by a tuning coefficient: Y~q,i​(λ^q,t)=Yq,i−λ^q,t​Yq,iLLM\tilde{Y}_{q,i}(\hat{\lambda}_{q,t})=Y_{q,i}-\hat{\lambda}_{q,t}\,Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q,i}, where λ^q,t\hat{\lambda}_{q,t} is the clipped sample regression coefficient Eq. (7) computed from all paired observations available for question qq at time tt. The unknown difficulty accordingly becomes Aq​(λq∗)=Var⁡(Yq−λq∗​YqLLM)A_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*})=\mathrm{Var}(Y_{q}-\lambda_{q}^{*}\,Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}), and the difficulty estimator is the sample variance of these tuned residuals.

  2. 2.

    UCB construction under joint uncertainty. This parametrization introduces an additional source of estimation noise, the coefficient λ^q,t\hat{\lambda}_{q,t} is itself learned, so the UCB must account for uncertainty in both the variance estimate and the tuning parameter.

  3. 3.

    PPI++ output estimator. At termination, the algorithm reports the PPI++ estimate for each question: θ^qPPI++=Y¯q,nq+λ^q,B​(Y¯q,mqLLM−Y¯q,nqLLM)\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{PPI++}}_{q}=\bar{Y}_{q,n_{q}}+\hat{\lambda}_{q,B}\big(\bar{Y}^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q,m_{q}}-\bar{Y}^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q,n_{q}}\big), where mq≫nqm_{q}\gg n_{q} and λ^q,B\hat{\lambda}_{q,B} is the final tuning coefficient at termination. Setting λ^q,B=1\hat{\lambda}_{q,B}=1 recovers the standard PPI output of Algorithm 1.

4.3 Regret Guarantee for PPI++

Define the oracle allocation by substituting Aq​(λq∗)A_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*}) into the offline rule:

nq∗=B∑j=1Qwj​Aj​(λj∗)​cj​wq​Aq​(λq∗)cq,Λ⁡(λ∗):=∑j=1Qwj​Aj​(λj∗)​cj.n_{q}^{*}=\frac{B}{\sum_{j=1}^{Q}\sqrt{w_{j}A_{j}(\lambda_{j}^{*})c_{j}}}\sqrt{\frac{w_{q}A_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*})}{c_{q}}},\qquad\Lambda(\lambda^{*}):=\sum_{j=1}^{Q}\sqrt{w_{j}A_{j}(\lambda_{j}^{*})c_{j}}.

Let nq,Bn_{q,B} denote the number of labels allocated to question qq by Algorithm 2. The regret is

ℛ⁡(B,λ∗):=E⁡[∑q=1Qwq​Aq​(λq∗)nq,B]−∑q=1Qwq​Aq​(λq∗)nq∗.\mathcal{R}(B;\lambda^{*}):=\mathrm{E}\!\left[\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\frac{w_{q}A_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*})}{n_{q,B}}\right]-\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\frac{w_{q}A_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*})}{n_{q}^{*}}. (8)

We impose two mild assumptions for the analysis, analogous to Assumptions 3.4–3.4 in the PPI case, with minor adjustments to accommodate the concentration of the tuning parameter λq∗\lambda_{q}^{*}.

{assumption}

For each q∈[Q]q\in[Q],

Yq∈[LY,UY],YqLLM∈[LYLLM,UYLLM]almost surely.Y_{q}\in[L_{Y},U_{Y}],\qquad Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}\in[L_{Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}},U_{Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}}]\qquad\text{almost surely.}

Define RY:=UY−LYR_{Y}:=U_{Y}-L_{Y}, RYLLM:=UYLLM−LYLLMR_{Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}}:=U_{Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}}-L_{Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}}, R:=RY+RYLLMR:=R_{Y}+R_{Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}}, MY:=max⁡(|LY|,|UY|)M_{Y}:=\max(|L_{Y}|,|U_{Y}|), and MYLLM:=max⁡(|LYLLM|,|UYLLM|)M_{Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}}:=\max(|L_{Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}}|,|U_{Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}}|). Then Y~q​(λ)\tilde{Y}_{q}(\lambda) has range at most RR for every λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1]. {assumption} We assume (i) Amin:=minq⁡Aq​(λq∗)>0A_{\min}:=\min_{q}A_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*})>0, where Aq​(λq∗):=Var⁡(Yq−λq∗​YqLLM)A_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*}):=\mathrm{Var}(Y_{q}-\lambda_{q}^{*}Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}), and (ii) for each q∈[Q]q\in[Q], Var⁡(YqLLM)≥VminLLM\mathrm{Var}(Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q})\geq V_{\min}^{\mathrm{LLM}} for some constant VminLLM>0V_{\min}^{\mathrm{LLM}}>0. Assumption 4.3 strengthens the bounded-residual condition (Assumption 3.4) by requiring YqY_{q} and YqLLMY^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q} to be individually bounded, which ensures uniform variance concentration over all λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1]. Assumption 4.3 extends the nondegeneracy condition (Assumption 3.4) to the PPI++ setting. Part (i) is the direct analogue: no question is perfectly predicted after tuning. Part (ii) additionally requires the LLM predictions to carry a nonvanishing signal, which is needed for the plug-in estimate λ^q,t\hat{\lambda}_{q,t} to concentrate around λq∗\lambda_{q}^{*}.

Algorithm 2 achieves the following regret guarantee.

Theorem 4.1

Assume Assumptions 4.3–4.3 hold. Run Algorithm 2 with K≥K0​⌈ln⁡(Q​Tmax/δ)⌉K\geq K_{0}\lceil\ln(QT_{\max}/\delta)\rceil, where K0K_{0} depends only on the parameters in Assumptions 4.3–4.3. Let Vmax​(λ∗):=∑q=1Qwq​Aq​(λq∗)/KV_{\max}(\lambda^{*}):=\sum_{q=1}^{Q}w_{q}A_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*})/K. Then for all sufficiently large BB,

ℛ⁡(B,λ∗)≤O⁡(ln⁡(Q​Tmax/δ)B2)+δ​Vmax​(λ∗).\mathcal{R}(B;\lambda^{*})\leq O\!\left(\frac{\ln(QT_{\max}/\delta)}{B^{2}}\right)+\delta V_{\max}(\lambda^{*}).

In particular, choosing δ=B−2\delta=B^{-2} yields ℛ⁡(B,λ∗)=O⁡(ln⁡BB2)\mathcal{R}(B;\lambda^{*})=O\!\left(\frac{\ln B}{B^{2}}\right).

Proof Sketch.

The complete proof is in Online Appendix C. The high-level ideas are identical to those of Theorem 3.1 after replacing AqA_{q} by Aq​(λq∗)A_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*}) and the UCB Aq,tUCBA^{\mathrm{UCB}}_{q,t} by its PPI++ analogue. Steps II–III (allocation-gap control and corresponding regret conversion) are similar. The nontrivial change is Step I, where we must ensure optimism despite the additional estimation error from the plug-in λ^q,t\hat{\lambda}_{q,t}. This requires two auxiliary concentration results: (i) a bound on |λ^q,t−λq∗||\hat{\lambda}_{q,t}-\lambda_{q}^{*}| via ratio perturbation (Lemma C.2), and (ii) uniform concentration of σ^q,t​(λ)\hat{\sigma}_{q,t}(\lambda) over λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] via a grid-and-Lipschitz argument (Lemma C.4). The combined PPI++ good event then holds with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, and the remainder of the proof follows as in the PPI case.

5 Synthetic Data Analysis

Next, we evaluate Algorithm 2 on a controlled synthetic environment. All experiments use 200 Monte Carlo replications; shaded bands in figures indicate ±1\pm 1 standard error across replications.

5.1 Experiment Setup

We simulate Q=100Q=100 survey questions with equal weights wq=1w_{q}=1 and equal costs cq=1c_{q}=1. Each question qq has a per-question variance scale vqv_{q} drawn from a log-uniform distribution to create heterogeneous difficulties:

vq=hsinh⁡h⋅eUq,Uq​∼i.i.d.​Uniform​(−h,h),v_{q}=\frac{h}{\sinh h}\cdot e^{U_{q}},\quad U_{q}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Uniform}(-h,h), (9)

where hh is a heterogeneity parameter controlling the spread of question difficulties. The scaling factor h/sinh⁡hh/\sinh h ensures E⁡[vq]=1\mathrm{E}[v_{q}]=1 for all hh, so varying hh redistributes difficulty across questions without changing the overall MSE scale. Since log⁡vq\log v_{q} is uniform on (−h,h)(-h,h), the standard deviation of log-difficulties is sd⁡(log⁡Aq)=h/3\mathrm{sd}(\log A_{q})=h/\sqrt{3} and the coefficient of variation of AqA_{q} is CV⁡(Aq)=h​coth⁡h−1\mathrm{CV}(A_{q})=\sqrt{h\coth h-1}. At the baseline h=2.0h=2.0, CV≈1.04\mathrm{CV}\approx 1.04, indicating substantial heterogeneity; at h=0.5h=0.5, CV≈0.29\mathrm{CV}\approx 0.29, a nearly homogeneous setting.

For each question qq, paired observations (Y,S)(Y,S) are generated from a bivariate Gaussian model with independent standard normals U,ε,η​∼i.i.d.​𝒩​(0,1)U,\varepsilon,\eta\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,1):

Ysig\displaystyle Y_{\mathrm{sig}} =vq​U,\displaystyle=\sqrt{v_{q}}\,U,
S\displaystyle S =vq​(ρ​U+1−ρ2​ε),\displaystyle=\sqrt{v_{q}}\bigl(\rho\,U+\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}\,\varepsilon\bigr),
Y\displaystyle Y =vq​(U+ση​η),\displaystyle=\sqrt{v_{q}}\bigl(U+\sigma_{\eta}\,\eta\bigr),

where YsigY_{\mathrm{sig}} is a latent signal, S=f⁡(X)S=f(X) is the LLM prediction correlated with the signal through ρ∈[0,1]\rho\in[0,1], and ση\sigma_{\eta} scales additional human response noise. This gives Var⁡(Ysig,q)=Var⁡(Sq)=vq\mathrm{Var}(Y_{\mathrm{sig},q})=\mathrm{Var}(S_{q})=v_{q} and Var⁡(Yq)=vq​(1+ση2)\mathrm{Var}(Y_{q})=v_{q}(1+\sigma_{\eta}^{2}). The true population mean is θq∗=0\theta_{q}^{*}=0 for all qq. Under this model, the optimal PPI++ tuning parameter is λq∗=ρ\lambda_{q}^{*}=\rho for all qq (since the LLM observes the signal but not the human noise), and the rectification difficulty is

Aq=vq​(1−ρ2+ση2).A_{q}=v_{q}(1-\rho^{2}+\sigma_{\eta}^{2}).

Since Aq∝vqA_{q}\propto v_{q}, questions with larger variance scale are harder to rectify and receive more samples under the oracle allocation Eq. (2). Table 1 summarizes the baseline parameters; Experiments 2 and 3 vary one parameter at a time.

We compare four allocation policies, all using the PPI++ estimator with plug-in λ^q\hat{\lambda}_{q} and no data splitting:

  1. (i)

    Oracle (Neyman): allocates proportional to Aq\sqrt{A_{q}} using the true difficulties, i.e., the offline optimum Eq. (2).

  2. (ii)

    Uniform: equal allocation across all questions, serving as a no-information baseline representing conventional survey sampling.

  3. (iii)

    ε\varepsilon-Greedy: a standard decaying ε\varepsilon-greedy policy from the bandit literature. At round tt, with probability εt=min⁡(1,c​Q/t)\varepsilon_{t}=\min(1,\,cQ/t) (where c=5c=5) a question is selected uniformly at random; otherwise the greedy choice qt=arg⁡maxq⁡A^q,t/nq,t2q_{t}=\arg\max_{q}\widehat{A}_{q,t}/n_{q,t}^{2} is made.

  4. (iv)

    UCB: Algorithm 2 with variance-adaptive confidence bounds, balancing exploitation and exploration.

To compare these policies, the primary metric throughout Sections 5–6 is the expected MSE at budget tt, defined as

MSE⁡(t):=∑q=1Qwq​Aqnq,t,\mathrm{MSE}(t)\;:=\;\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{n_{q,t}}, (10)

evaluated at each budget step in Figure 1 and at the terminal budget BB in all subsequent figures and tables. In the equal-weight baseline (wq=1w_{q}=1 for all qq), this reduces to ∑qAq/nq,t\sum_{q}A_{q}/n_{q,t}. This is the natural performance measure for two reasons. First, it is the quantity that appears in the regret definition (Eqs. (4) and (8)): the regret ℛ⁡(B)=MSE⁡(B)−MSE∗​(B)\mathcal{R}(B)=\mathrm{MSE}(B)-\mathrm{MSE}^{*}(B) directly compares each policy’s expected MSE to the oracle MSE∗​(B)=(∑qwq​Aq​cq)2/B\mathrm{MSE}^{*}(B)=(\sum_{q}\sqrt{w_{q}A_{q}c_{q}})^{2}/B, so reporting expected MSE aligns the empirical evaluation with the theory. Second, in the SDR regime, ∑qwq​Aq/nq,t\sum_{q}w_{q}A_{q}/n_{q,t} is the oracle allocation objective implied by the asymptotic variance formula. For the plug-in PPI++ implementation used in our experiments, we therefore interpret this quantity as an allocation-quality metric rather than the exact finite-sample conditional MSE of the estimator.

5.2 Numerical Results

Experiment 1: Policy comparison (Q=100Q{=}100, B=2,000B{=}2{,}000, ρ=0.7\rho{=}0.7, h=2.0h{=}2.0). Figure 1 reports results at the baseline parameters. At the terminal budget B=2,000B=2{,}000, the oracle achieves an expected MSE of 2.628; UCB attains 2.712, ε\varepsilon-greedy 2.857, and uniform 3.529. Measuring the percentage gap to oracle, (MSE−MSE∗)/MSE∗(\mathrm{MSE}-\mathrm{MSE}^{*})/\mathrm{MSE}^{*}, UCB is within 3.2%, ε\varepsilon-greedy 8.8%, and uniform 34.4%. The left panel shows how the expected MSE decreases as budget is spent; UCB tracks the oracle closely after the initialization phase (K⋅Q=300K\cdot Q=300 samples), whereas ε\varepsilon-greedy converges more slowly. The center panel (log–log scale) confirms that UCB converges to the oracle rate. The right panel plots the terminal regret of UCB alone across budgets B∈{500, 1,000, 2,000, 5,000, 10,000}B\in\{500,\,1{,}000,\,2{,}000,\,5{,}000,\,10{,}000\}, showing that UCB regret is consistent with an O⁡(ln⁡B/B2)O(\ln B/B^{2}) rate, with an empirical log–log slope near −2-2.

UCB dominates all other policies at every budget level. The ε\varepsilon-greedy policy outperforms uniform only when the budget is sufficiently large (at B=2,000B=2{,}000 it achieves an 8.8% gap versus uniform’s 34.4%, but at B=1,000B=1{,}000 it is slightly worse), because its undirected exploration phase consumes a large share of the budget before exploitation begins. UCB, by contrast, directs exploration through variance-adaptive confidence bounds, building reliable AqA_{q} estimates faster.

Having established UCB’s overall advantage, we next examine how LLM quality and difficulty heterogeneity affect performance.

Experiment 2: Effect of LLM quality (B=1,000B{=}1{,}000, varying ρ\rho). Figure 2 varies ρ∈{0.0,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9,0.95}\rho\in\{0.0,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9,0.95\}. Higher ρ\rho reduces the expected MSE for all policies equally, because Aq=vq​(1−ρ2+ση2)A_{q}=v_{q}(1-\rho^{2}+\sigma_{\eta}^{2}) scales all difficulties by the same factor. The relative gap between policies is stable across ρ\rho: this stability is a consequence of the synthetic design, in which ρ\rho is a global parameter that preserves the heterogeneity structure. In real surveys, LLM quality varies across question types (see Section 6, where λq∗\lambda_{q}^{*} ranges from 00 to 0.720.72); the digital twin experiments provide a more demanding test.

Experiment 3: Effect of heterogeneity (B=1,000B{=}1{,}000, varying hh). Figure 3 varies h∈{0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0}h\in\{0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0\} and reveals the central insight: the value of adaptive allocation is determined by difficulty heterogeneity. When questions are nearly homogeneous (h=0.5h=0.5), uniform allocation is near-optimal and adaptive methods incur unnecessary exploration cost. As heterogeneity increases, uniform’s gap grows from 2.2% to 34.4%, while UCB’s gap grows only from 6.2% to 8.1%, because its directed exploration successfully tracks the increasingly non-uniform oracle allocation.

6 Digital-Twin Data Analysis

We now evaluate the UCB allocation algorithm on real survey data from the Twin-2K-500 dataset (Toubia et al. 2025), a large-scale digital twin benchmark in which each human respondent is paired with an LLM-generated “digital twin.” This provides a realistic testbed where the rectification difficulties {Aq}\{A_{q}\} arise from genuine human-LLM disagreement patterns rather than a parametric data-generating process.

6.1 Data and Setup

The Twin-2K-500 dataset contains four survey waves administered to over 2,000 US respondents. Waves 1–3 each cover around 500 questions spanning demographics, psychological scales, cognitive tasks, and behavioral economics. Wave 4 re-administers a subset of questions to the same respondent panel for test-retest reliability assessment. Following the same evaluation protocol of Toubia et al. (2025), we focus on the Wave 4 retest battery and restrict attention to multiple-choice questions. This yields Q=68Q=68 questions across 14 task types, with between 651 and 2,058 respondents per question (mean 1,271). The dataset provides paired LLM responses generated by GPT-4o from each respondent’s “digital twin” profile. Human and LLM responses are min-max scaled to [0,1][0,1] following the same data processing. We compute the full-sample rectification difficulty Aq=Var⁡(Yq−λq∗​YqLLM)A_{q}=\mathrm{Var}(Y_{q}-\lambda_{q}^{*}Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}) for each question, where λq∗=Cov⁡(Yq,YqLLM)/Var⁡(YqLLM)\lambda_{q}^{*}=\mathrm{Cov}(Y_{q},Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q})/\mathrm{Var}(Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}), clipped to [0,1][0,1], is the optimal PPI++ tuning parameter.

Figure 4 plots each question’s rectification difficulty AqA_{q} against its optimal PPI++ tuning parameter λq∗\lambda_{q}^{*}, colored by task type. Two features stand out. First, difficulties are heterogeneous (AqA_{q} ranges from 0.0240.024 to 0.2390.239, CV =0.63=0.63). Second, 38% of questions have λq∗≈0\lambda_{q}^{*}\approx 0, meaning the LLM signal does not reduce residual variance for those items.

Experiment setup.

We evaluate the same four policies as in Section 5.1: Oracle, Uniform, ε\varepsilon-greedy, and UCB. In addition, we introduce a fifth policy, Explore-then-Commit (ETC), which operationalizes the natural “pilot study” approach from survey practice. ETC allocates a fraction α\alpha of the post-initialization budget uniformly across all questions to estimate {Aq}\{A_{q}\}, then commits the remaining budget to the Neyman allocation nq∝wq​A^q/cqn_{q}\propto\sqrt{w_{q}\widehat{A}_{q}/c_{q}} computed from the pilot estimates. We use α=0.3\alpha=0.3 as the default and examine sensitivity to α\alpha below. At each replication, human–LLM pairs are drawn with replacement from the respondent pool, simulating the sequential survey process on real data. As in Section 5, we report the expected MSE Eq. (10) evaluated at the terminal budget BB. All experiments use 500 Monte Carlo replications.

6.2 Policy Comparison

As in Section 5, we evaluate all policies using the expected MSE ∑qwq​Aq/nq​(B)\sum_{q}w_{q}A_{q}/n_{q}(B), which measures allocation quality at the terminal budget using the true AqA_{q} values. Table 2 reports this metric across budgets B∈{500,1,000,1,500,2,000}B\in\{500,1{,}000,1{,}500,2{,}000\}, along with each policy’s gap to oracle in parentheses.

UCB achieves the lowest MSE among all implementable policies at every budget level. At B=1,000B=1{,}000, the ordering is UCB (3.9% gap to oracle), ε\varepsilon-greedy (6.2%), uniform (10.6%), and ETC (19.7%). UCB’s gap decreases monotonically with budget, from 5.5% at B=500B=500 to 2.1% at B=2,000B=2{,}000, while uniform’s gap remains stable near 10–12%, reflecting its structural inability to adapt. The ε\varepsilon-greedy policy performs particularly poorly at small budgets (19.8% gap at B=500B=500) because its undirected exploration phase consumes most of the budget before exploitation begins; it overtakes uniform only above B=1,000B=1{,}000. ETC with pilot fraction α=0.3\alpha=0.3 is consistently worse than uniform, because the pilot phase provides only ∼ 6{\sim}\,6 samples per question, too few to estimate {Aq}\{A_{q}\} reliably. ETC is also sensitive to α\alpha: it requires α≥0.4\alpha\geq 0.4 to match uniform (see Table 6 in the Online Appendix), meaning a substantial share of the budget must be spent on undirected pilot sampling before any informed allocation begins.

We interpret the gap to oracle as wasted budget: a policy with a 10% gap produces the same estimation error as the oracle would with only 90% of the budget, effectively wasting the remaining 10%. Under this interpretation, uniform allocation wastes 10–12% of the human-labeling budget at every budget level, whereas UCB wastes only 2–6%. At B=2,000B=2{,}000, UCB’s waste shrinks to just 2.1%, meaning it operates near the efficiency frontier despite having no prior knowledge of question-level LLM accuracy.

To understand where UCB’s gains come from, we group the 68 questions by whether the LLM provides useful signal: 32 “LLM-weak” questions where λq∗<0.05\lambda_{q}^{*}<0.05 and 36 “LLM-useful” questions where λq∗≥0.05\lambda_{q}^{*}\geq 0.05. For LLM-useful questions, the plug-in λ\lambda shrinks AqA_{q} by absorbing LLM-predictable variance, leaving these questions with low residual difficulty. LLM-weak questions, by contrast, retain high AqA_{q} and dominate the total estimation error. The oracle allocation directs 56% of the budget to the LLM-weak group, compared to uniform’s 47% (=32/68=32/68). UCB learns this imbalance online and shifts budget toward the high-AqA_{q} questions that uniform allocation under-serves.

6.3 Weight and Cost Sensitivity

In practice, questions may differ in importance or sampling cost. We examine sensitivity to these factors by varying the dispersion parameter a∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0}a\in\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\} for importance weights (panel a: wq=1+a⋅zqw_{q}=1+a\cdot z_{q}, zq∼Uniform⁡(−1,1)z_{q}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(-1,1), clipped to [0,2][0,2], cq=1c_{q}=1) and sampling costs (panel b: same construction applied to cqc_{q}, wq=1w_{q}=1), fixing B=1,000B=1{,}000.

Table 3 shows that UCB maintains a stable gap of approximately 4% regardless of weight or cost dispersion, while uniform allocation degrades sharply (from 10.6% to 27.9% under heterogeneous weights) because it ignores both importance and cost structure. UCB’s Neyman-style index automatically concentrates budget on questions that are both important and hard to rectify.

6.4 Effect of Difficulty Heterogeneity

We rescale the spread of rectification difficulties using a log-space transformation that mirrors the synthetic DGP Eq. (9):

log⁡Aq(h)=log⁡A¯+h⋅(log⁡Aq−log⁡A¯),\log A_{q}^{(h)}=\overline{\log A}+h\cdot(\log A_{q}-\overline{\log A}), (11)

where log⁡A¯=Q−1​∑qlog⁡Aq\overline{\log A}=Q^{-1}\sum_{q}\log A_{q} is the mean log-difficulty and h≥0h\geq 0 controls heterogeneity. The resulting Aq(h)A_{q}^{(h)} are then renormalized so that A¯(h)=A¯\bar{A}^{(h)}=\bar{A}, preserving the overall MSE scale. At h=0h=0 all difficulties are equal; h=1h=1 recovers the original data; h>1h>1 amplifies heterogeneity.

Table 4 reports the terminal regret (absolute, not percentage) for each policy. When difficulties are homogeneous (h=0h=0), uniform allocation is oracle-optimal and both UCB and ε\varepsilon-greedy incur unnecessary exploration cost. As heterogeneity grows, the benefit of adaptive allocation increases sharply: uniform regret rises from near zero to 14.2214.22 (×10−2\times 10^{-2}), while UCB regret grows only from 0.950.95 to 4.124.12 (4-fold). ETC regret is nearly constant across heterogeneity levels (∼ 8.7{\sim}\,8.7–9.19.1), because the noisy pilot estimates produce similarly suboptimal commit allocations regardless of the underlying difficulty structure. The comparison with the synthetic heterogeneity experiment (Section 5.2) is instructive: on the real data, the same qualitative pattern holds (UCB’s advantage grows monotonically with heterogeneity), but the absolute magnitudes are smaller, reflecting the more moderate difficulty distribution in real surveys.

6.5 Module-Level Allocation

As discussed in Section 2.1, many surveys assign respondents to question modules rather than individual questions. We demonstrate that the UCB algorithm applies directly at this coarser level. We group the 68 questions into Q=14Q=14 task-type modules (e.g., “Anchoring” with 4 questions, “Probability Matching” with 16 questions). Each budget unit allocates one respondent to a module, and that respondent answers all questions in the module, so the module-level difficulty is Aw=∑q∈wAqA_{w}=\sum_{q\in w}A_{q} (a sum, not an average, because each respondent contributes one observation to every question in the module). The resulting AwA_{w} values range from 0.080.08 to 2.712.71, exhibiting substantial heterogeneity.

With Q=14Q=14 modules and budget B=200B=200 respondent-module assignments (approximately 14 per module under uniform allocation), UCB achieves a 3.8% gap to oracle, closely matching its 3.9% gap in the question-level experiment (Table 2). Uniform allocation incurs a 29.7% gap, while ETC (9.1%) and ε\varepsilon-greedy (10.6%) fall between. The same algorithm applies without modification because the Aw/nwA_{w}/n_{w} objective structure is preserved.

Together, these experiments confirm that the theoretical advantages of UCB-based adaptive allocation demonstrated on synthetic data carry over to a real survey environment: UCB consistently achieves the smallest regret among all implementable policies, outperforming not only uniform allocation and ε\varepsilon-greedy but also the explore-then-commit approach that operationalizes the natural pilot-study heuristic. UCB adapts to heterogeneous weights and costs, and scales its advantage with the degree of difficulty heterogeneity across questions. Moreover, the framework applies equally well at coarser operational units: when allocation targets are survey modules rather than individual questions, UCB continues to track the oracle closely.

7 Conclusion

This paper studies a resource allocation problem that arises when generative AI is deployed as a low-cost prediction layer but human verification remains the ground truth: how to allocate scarce human oversight across tasks when AI reliability varies and is unknown before deployment. We develop a UCB-based online algorithm that learns where human effort is most needed while allocating the budget, with formal regret guarantees. Experiments on LLM-augmented surveys confirm that the algorithm substantially outperforms uniform allocation, pilot-study approaches, and standard bandit baselines. The framework extends to module-level allocation and to general MM-estimation targets, including regression coefficients and conjoint partworths (Online Appendix A), with a synthetic MNL experiment validating the extension.

More broadly, the same principle applies whenever AI generates cheap but unevenly reliable outputs across tasks and humans provide the ground truth. The operational value of generative AI depends not only on model capability but also on how the surrounding human-oversight system is designed. Future directions include batched allocation for panel survey operations, adaptation to model drift, and settings where human feedback triggers model updates or escalation policies.

Online Appendix: Adaptive Budget Allocation in LLM-Augmented Surveys

Appendix A Extension to General MM-Estimation

The main text focuses on population means (θq∗=E⁡[Yq]\theta_{q}^{*}=\mathrm{E}[Y_{q}]), but many survey applications target richer estimands such as category choice probabilities, regression coefficients, or conjoint partworths. Here we show that the Aq/nqA_{q}/n_{q} variance structure, and therefore the entire UCB allocation framework, carries over to any estimand defined through an MM-estimation problem, once the multi-dimensional asymptotic covariance is reduced to a scalar difficulty index. We fix a question qq and suppress subscripts throughout, writing 𝒫\mathcal{P}, 𝜽∗\bm{\theta}^{*}, dd, nn, etc.

A.1 Setup and examples

Consider a convex, twice-differentiable loss ℓ⁡(𝑿,Y,𝜽)\ell(\bm{X},Y;\bm{\theta}) whose population risk has a unique minimizer 𝜽∗=\argmin𝜽∈ℝd​E​[ℓ⁡(𝑿,Y,𝜽)]\bm{\theta}^{*}=\argmin_{\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\,\mathrm{E}[\ell(\bm{X},Y;\bm{\theta})], with score function 𝝍⁡(𝑿,Y,𝜽):=∇𝜽ℓ​(𝑿,Y,𝜽)\bm{\psi}(\bm{X},Y;\bm{\theta}):=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\ell(\bm{X},Y;\bm{\theta}) satisfying E⁡[𝝍⁡(𝑿,Y,𝜽∗)]=𝟎\mathrm{E}[\bm{\psi}(\bm{X},Y;\bm{\theta}^{*})]=\bm{0}. Let 𝑯:=E⁡[∇𝜽𝝍​(𝑿,Y,𝜽∗)]\bm{H}:=\mathrm{E}[\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\bm{\psi}(\bm{X},Y;\bm{\theta}^{*})] denote the nonsingular population Hessian.

This setup covers four common cases. (i) Mean estimation: d=1d=1, ℓ=12​(Y−θ)2\ell=\tfrac{1}{2}(Y-\theta)^{2}, recovering θ∗=E⁡[Y]\theta^{*}=\mathrm{E}[Y]. (ii) Categorical responses: for Y∈{1,…,K}Y\in\{1,\dots,K\}, the loss ℓ=∑k12(1{Y=k}−θk)2\ell=\sum_{k}\tfrac{1}{2}(\text{1}\{Y{=}k\}-\theta_{k})^{2} yields category probabilities θk∗=Pr⁡(Y=k)\theta_{k}^{*}=\Pr(Y{=}k). (iii) Linear regression: ℓ=12​(Y−𝑿⊤​𝜽)2\ell=\tfrac{1}{2}(Y-\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{\theta})^{2} gives 𝜽∗=E​[𝑿​𝑿⊤]−1​E​[𝑿​Y]\bm{\theta}^{*}=\mathrm{E}[\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}]^{-1}\mathrm{E}[\bm{X}Y]. (iv) Multinomial logit: the MNL negative log-likelihood ℓ=log(∑ke𝑿k⊤​𝜽)−∑k(𝑿k⊤𝜽)1{Y=k}\ell=\log(\sum_{k}e^{\bm{X}_{k}^{\top}\bm{\theta}})-\sum_{k}(\bm{X}_{k}^{\top}\bm{\theta})\text{1}\{Y{=}k\} yields conjoint partworths.

A.2 PPI++ MM-estimator and variance structure

Given an LLM predictor f⁡(𝑿)f(\bm{X}), define the surrogate score 𝝍LLM​(𝑿,𝜽):=𝝍⁡(𝑿,f⁡(𝑿),𝜽)\bm{\psi}^{\mathrm{LLM}}(\bm{X};\bm{\theta}):=\bm{\psi}(\bm{X},f(\bm{X});\bm{\theta}). For tuning parameter λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1], the PPI++ MM-estimator solves

𝟎=1n​∑i=1n𝝍⁡(𝑿i,Yi,𝜽)+λ⁡(E⁡[𝝍LLM​(𝑿,𝜽)]−1n​∑i=1n𝝍LLM​(𝑿i,𝜽)),\bm{0}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{\psi}(\bm{X}_{i},Y_{i};\bm{\theta})+\lambda\left(\mathrm{E}[\bm{\psi}^{\mathrm{LLM}}(\bm{X};\bm{\theta})]-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{\psi}^{\mathrm{LLM}}(\bm{X}_{i};\bm{\theta})\right), (12)

where the expectation is approximated from a large synthetic pool. Because the surrogate terms cancel at 𝜽∗\bm{\theta}^{*}, the estimator is consistent for any λ\lambda regardless of LLM misspecification.

In the synthetic-data-rich regime, linearizing Eq. (12) around 𝜽∗\bm{\theta}^{*} yields n​(𝜽^​(λ)−𝜽∗)→𝑑𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝚺⁡(λ))\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\bm{\theta}}(\lambda)-\bm{\theta}^{*})\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{\Sigma}(\lambda)), where the sandwich covariance is

𝚺⁡(λ)=𝑯−1​𝑽Δ⁡(λ)​𝑯−⁣⊤,𝑽Δ⁡(λ):=Var⁡(𝝍⁡(𝑿,Y,𝜽∗)−λ​𝝍LLM​(𝑿,𝜽∗)).\bm{\Sigma}(\lambda)=\bm{H}^{-1}\bm{V}^{\Delta(\lambda)}\bm{H}^{-\top},\qquad\bm{V}^{\Delta(\lambda)}:=\mathrm{Var}\!\big(\bm{\psi}(\bm{X},Y;\bm{\theta}^{*})-\lambda\,\bm{\psi}^{\mathrm{LLM}}(\bm{X};\bm{\theta}^{*})\big).

As in the scalar case, Var⁡(𝜽^​(λ))≈𝚺⁡(λ)/n\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\bm{\theta}}(\lambda))\approx\bm{\Sigma}(\lambda)/n: the labeled sample size nn enters only through a 1/n1/n prefactor.

A.3 Scalar difficulty index for allocation

The allocation framework requires a scalar difficulty per question. Two standard design criteria reduce 𝚺⁡(λ)\bm{\Sigma}(\lambda) to a scalar while preserving the 1/n1/n structure. The A-optimal (trace) criterion defines A(A)​(λ):=tr⁡(𝛀​𝚺​(λ))A^{(A)}(\lambda):=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{\Omega}\,\bm{\Sigma}(\lambda)) for a weight matrix 𝛀=𝑳⊤​𝑳⪰𝟎\bm{\Omega}=\bm{L}^{\top}\bm{L}\succeq\bm{0} reflecting which linear functions of 𝜽\bm{\theta} matter most. The D-optimal (determinant) criterion defines A(D)​(λ):=det(𝚺⁡(λ))1/dA^{(D)}(\lambda):=\det(\bm{\Sigma}(\lambda))^{1/d}, which is reparameterization-invariant. Under either criterion, the per-question objective takes the form A⁡(λ)/nA(\lambda)/n, so the UCB allocation algorithm and its regret guarantee apply directly after replacing the scalar rectification difficulty with the chosen scalarization.

A.4 Numerical illustration: MNL partworth estimation

We verify the above framework with a synthetic multinomial logit (MNL) experiment. Consider Q=50Q=50 choice tasks, each with K=3K=3 alternatives and d=2d=2-dimensional partworths. For each task qq, alternatives have features 𝑿q∈ℝK×d\bm{X}_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d} constructed from a rotated balanced design scaled by a per-question factor sqs_{q}, where {sq}\{s_{q}\} are drawn from the same log-uniform distribution as in Eq. (9) with h=1.0h=1.0. True partworths 𝜷q∗\bm{\beta}_{q}^{*} are unit-norm random directions, and LLM partworths are generated as 𝜷qLLM=ρ​𝜷q∗+𝜺q\bm{\beta}_{q}^{\mathrm{LLM}}=\rho\,\bm{\beta}_{q}^{*}+\bm{\varepsilon}_{q} with ρ=0.7\rho=0.7 and 𝜺q∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,0.32​𝑰d)\bm{\varepsilon}_{q}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},0.3^{2}\bm{I}_{d}). Human and LLM choices are sampled from MNL⁡(𝑿q,𝜷q∗)\mathrm{MNL}(\bm{X}_{q},\bm{\beta}_{q}^{*}) and MNL⁡(𝑿q,𝜷qLLM)\mathrm{MNL}(\bm{X}_{q},\bm{\beta}_{q}^{\mathrm{LLM}}), respectively.

For each task, we compute the scalar difficulty Aq=tr⁡(𝑯q−1​𝑽qΔ​𝑯q−⁣⊤)A_{q}=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{H}_{q}^{-1}\bm{V}_{q}^{\Delta}\bm{H}_{q}^{-\top}) via Monte Carlo with 50,000 samples, where 𝑯q\bm{H}_{q} is the MNL Hessian and 𝑽qΔ\bm{V}_{q}^{\Delta} is the score residual covariance. The resulting AqA_{q} values range from 4.84.8 to 39.739.7 (coefficient of variation 0.720.72), reflecting substantial heterogeneity driven by the feature scaling.

We then run the allocation experiment with budget B=2,000B=2{,}000, initialization K0=3K_{0}=3, and 200200 replications.

Table 5 confirms that the UCB allocation framework extends to vector-valued MM-estimation targets. UCB achieves a 2.0% gap to oracle, comparable to the mean-estimation results in Sections 5–6, while uniform allocation wastes 13.1% of its budget. The allocation mechanism depends only on the scalar difficulties {Aq}\{A_{q}\}, so the UCB algorithm applies without modification once AqA_{q} is computed from the sandwich covariance.

which is O⁡(B​ln⁡(1/δ))O(\sqrt{B\ln(1/\delta)}). □\square

B.3 Step III: Convert the Allocation Gaps into Regret Bound

To bound the regret ℛ⁡(B)\mathcal{R}(B), we convert the allocation gaps in Step II into the objective deviation using the Taylor expansion of fq​(n)=wq​Aqnf_{q}(n)=\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{n}. By Taylor’s theorem, there exists ξq\xi_{q} between nq,Bn_{q,B} and nq∗n_{q}^{*} such that:

fq​(nq,B)−fq​(nq∗)=−wq​Aq(nq∗)2​(nq,B−nq∗)+wq​Aqξq3​(nq,B−nq∗)2.f_{q}(n_{q,B})-f_{q}(n_{q}^{*})=-\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{(n_{q}^{*})^{2}}(n_{q,B}-n_{q}^{*})+\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{\xi_{q}^{3}}(n_{q,B}-n_{q}^{*})^{2}. (15)

Analysis of Term 1: By the optimality condition wq​Aq(nq∗)2=λ⁡(B)​cq\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{(n_{q}^{*})^{2}}=\lambda(B)c_{q}, where λ⁡(B)=(∑jwj​Aj​cj)2B2\lambda(B)=\frac{(\sum_{j}\sqrt{w_{j}A_{j}c_{j}})^{2}}{B^{2}}, we have:

Term 1=−λ(B)∑q=1Qcq(nq,B−nq∗)=λ(B)(B−∑q=1Qcqnq,B).\text{Term 1}=-\lambda(B)\sum_{q=1}^{Q}c_{q}(n_{q,B}-n_{q}^{*})=\lambda(B)(B-\sum_{q=1}^{Q}c_{q}n_{q,B}). (17)

Since the algorithm terminates only when the remaining budget is less than cmax=maxq⁡cqc_{\max}=\max_{q}c_{q}, recall that RemB=B−∑cq​nq,B∈[0,cmax)\text{Rem}_{B}=B-\sum c_{q}n_{q,B}\in[0,c_{\max}). Thus:

Term 1≤(∑jwj​Aj​cj)2B2​cmax.\text{Term 1}\leq\frac{(\sum_{j}\sqrt{w_{j}A_{j}c_{j}})^{2}}{B^{2}}c_{\max}. (18)

Since |nq,B−nq∗|≤O⁡(B)|n_{q,B}-n_{q}^{*}|\leq O(\sqrt{B}), there exists a budget threshold B0B_{0} that ensures that for all B≥B0B\geq B_{0}, |nq,B−nq∗|≤12​B​βq|n_{q,B}-n_{q}^{*}|\leq\frac{1}{2}B\beta_{q}.

Analysis of Term 2: For all B≥B0B\geq B_{0}, the condition ξq≥12​nq∗\xi_{q}\geq\frac{1}{2}n_{q}^{*} holds almost surely on the good event ℰ\mathcal{E}.

For B≥B0B\geq B_{0}, by the conclusion in step II, Term 2 from the Taylor expansion is bounded by:

Term 2≤∑q=1Q8​wq​Aq(B​βq)3​(nq,B−nq∗)2≤C1B3​∑q=1Qwq​Aqβq3​βq2​(2​R​2​B​ln⁡(2/δq,B)Amin​βmin)2.\text{Term 2}\leq\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\frac{8w_{q}A_{q}}{(B\beta_{q})^{3}}(n_{q,B}-n_{q}^{*})^{2}\leq\frac{C_{1}}{B^{3}}\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{\beta_{q}^{3}}\beta_{q}^{2}\left(\frac{2R\sqrt{2B\ln(2/\delta_{q,B})}}{\sqrt{A_{\min}\beta_{\min}}}\right)^{2}. (19)

Final Regret Bound: With δ=B−2\delta=B^{-2}, in Lemma 3.2, P⁡(ℰc)≤B−2\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{E}^{c})\leq B^{-2}. On ℰc\mathcal{E}^{c}, the gap is bounded by Vmax=∑wq​AqKV_{\max}=\sum\frac{w_{q}A_{q}}{K}. Combining all components: the total expected regret ℛ⁡(B)\mathcal{R}(B) is:

Appendix C Proof of Theorem 4.1

The proof structure is identical to that of Theorem 3.1: only Step I (the good-event construction) changes to account for the additional estimation error from the plug-in λ^q,t\hat{\lambda}_{q,t}. Steps II–III carry over verbatim with AqA_{q} replaced by Aq​(λq∗)A_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*}).

C.1 Step I for PPI++: Define the Good Event and Bound its Probability

Recall YqLLM:=YqLLM=f⁡(Xq)Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}:=Y_{q}^{\mathrm{LLM}}=f(X_{q}) and the tuned residual Y~q​(λ):=Yq−λ​YqLLM\tilde{Y}_{q}(\lambda):=Y_{q}-\lambda Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}. Let

Aq​(λq∗):=Var⁡(Y~q​(λq∗)),λq∗:=Π[0,1]​(Cov⁡(Yq,YqLLM)Var⁡(YqLLM)).A_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*}):=\mathrm{Var}(\tilde{Y}_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*})),\qquad\lambda_{q}^{*}:=\Pi_{[0,1]}\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(Y_{q},Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q})}{\mathrm{Var}(Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q})}\right).

At time tt, the algorithm forms the plug-in estimator

λ^q,t:=Π[0,1]​(Cov^t​(Yq,YqLLM)Var^t​(YqLLM)),A^q,t​(λ^q,t):=Var^t​(Yq−λ^q,t​YqLLM),\hat{\lambda}_{q,t}:=\Pi_{[0,1]}\!\left(\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_{t}(Y_{q},Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q})}{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{t}(Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q})}\right),\qquad\widehat{A}_{q,t}(\hat{\lambda}_{q,t}):=\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{t}\!\big(Y_{q}-\hat{\lambda}_{q,t}Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}_{q}\big),

where Var^t​(⋅)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{t}(\cdot) and Cov^t​(⋅)\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_{t}(\cdot) denote the unbiased sample variance and covariance based on the nq,tn_{q,t} paired samples collected for question qq up to time tt. As in the PPI case, we distinguish notationally between fixed-sample-size statistics (indexed by ss) and adaptive-time statistics (indexed by tt): we write λ~q,s\tilde{\lambda}_{q,s} and σ~q,s​(λ)\tilde{\sigma}_{q,s}(\lambda) for the plug-in tuning parameter and sample standard deviation computed from the first ss i.i.d. pairs of question qq, and reserve λ^q,t\hat{\lambda}_{q,t} and A^q,t\widehat{A}_{q,t} for the same quantities evaluated at adaptive time tt (with nq,tn_{q,t} pairs). The two are related by λ^q,t=λ~q,nq,t\hat{\lambda}_{q,t}=\tilde{\lambda}_{q,n_{q,t}} and A^q,t​(λ^q,t)=A~q,nq,t​(λ~q,nq,t)\widehat{A}_{q,t}(\hat{\lambda}_{q,t})=\widetilde{A}_{q,n_{q,t}}(\tilde{\lambda}_{q,n_{q,t}}). Set Tmax:=⌊B/cmin⌋T_{\max}:=\lfloor B/c_{\min}\rfloor and δq,s:=δ/(Q​Tmax)\delta_{q,s}:=\delta/(QT_{\max}). Define the radius

ρq,s+⁣+:=R​2​ln⁡(4​(Tmax+1)/δq,s)s−1+2​RYLLMTmax+RYLLM2​Δλ​(s,δq,s/2),\rho^{++}_{q,s}:=R\sqrt{\frac{2\ln\!\big(4(T_{\max}+1)/\delta_{q,s}\big)}{s-1}}+\frac{\sqrt{2}\,R_{Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}}}{T_{\max}}+\frac{R_{Y^{\mathrm{LLM}}}}{2}\,\Delta_{\lambda}\!\big(s,\delta_{q,s}/2\big), (20)

where Δλ​(⋅,⋅)\Delta_{\lambda}(\cdot,\cdot) will be specified in Eq. (21). We define the PPI++ good event as

ℰ+⁣+:=⋂q=1Q⋂s=KTmax{|Aq​(λq∗)−A~q,s​(λ~q,s)|≤ρq,s+⁣+}.\mathcal{E}^{++}:=\bigcap_{q=1}^{Q}\bigcap_{s=K}^{T_{\max}}\left\{\left|\sqrt{A_{q}(\lambda_{q}^{*})}-\sqrt{\widetilde{A}_{q,s}(\tilde{\lambda}_{q,s})}\right|\leq\rho^{++}_{q,s}\right\}.
Lemma C.1

Under Assumptions 4.3 and 4.3, if K≥K0​⌈ln⁡(Q​Tmax/δ)⌉K\geq K_{0}\lceil\ln(QT_{\max}/\delta)\rceil where K0K_{0} depends only on the parameters in Assumptions 4.3–4.3, then

P⁡(ℰ+⁣+)≥1−δ.\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{E}^{++})\geq 1-\delta.

The explicit choice of K0K_{0} is given in Section C.1.2 below. This logarithmic initialization is required for the concentration of λ~\tilde{\lambda} for theoretical purposes and does not affect the O⁡(ln⁡B/B2)O(\ln B/B^{2}) regret rate. In Step II, the allocation gap is Δq,B=βq​(∑jcj​K+cmax+O⁡(B​ln⁡B))\Delta_{q,B}=\beta_{q}(\sum_{j}c_{j}K+c_{\max}+O(\sqrt{B\ln B})); the term ∑jcj​K=O⁡(Q​ln⁡B)\sum_{j}c_{j}K=O(Q\ln B) is dominated by O⁡(B​ln⁡B)O(\sqrt{B\ln B}), so Δq,B=O⁡(B​ln⁡B)\Delta_{q,B}=O(\sqrt{B\ln B}) as before. In Step III, the bad-event contribution δ⋅Vmax​(λ∗)=δ⋅O⁡(1/ln⁡B)=O⁡(1/(B2​ln⁡B))\delta\cdot V_{\max}(\lambda^{*})=\delta\cdot O(1/\ln B)=O(1/(B^{2}\ln B)) under δ=B−2\delta=B^{-2} is dominated by the O⁡(ln⁡B/B2)O(\ln B/B^{2}) main term.

The proof of Lemma C.1 combines two auxiliary results whose detailed proofs are deferred to the next subsubsection. First, Lemma C.2 establishes the concentration of the plug-in tuning parameter λ~q,s\tilde{\lambda}_{q,s} around its population counterpart λq∗\lambda_{q}^{*}, yielding the explicit deviation bound Δλ\Delta_{\lambda}. Second, Lemma C.4 provides a uniform concentration inequality for the standard deviation function σ~q,s​(λ)\tilde{\sigma}_{q,s}(\lambda) over all λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1], which accounts for both the grid-discretization error and the within-grid-point sampling error. Combining these two lemmas with a triangle inequality and a union bound over all (q,s)(q,s) pairs gives P⁡(ℰ+⁣+)≥1−δ\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{E}^{++})\geq 1-\delta, which is presented in Section C.1.2.
